nameStory: The "two-spotted" part of this bee's name comes from distinctive markings that help distinguish it from its many longhorn bee cousins. The "longhorn" refers to the impressively long antennae of the males, which can be nearly as long as their entire body and wave around like tiny fishing rods as they fly.
description: The Two-spotted Longhorn Bee is a medium-sized native bee that's part of our important wild pollinator community. These fuzzy, robust bees are excellent pollinators that visit a wide variety of flowers throughout the summer. Males are easily recognized by their extraordinarily long antennae, while females have shorter antennae but are often seen with their legs dusty with pollen. They're solitary bees, meaning each female builds her own nest rather than living in a hive like honeybees.

idTips.label: Male antennae
idTips.description: Males have dramatically long, thread-like antennae that extend well beyond their head - often nearly as long as their entire body and constantly moving as they fly

idTips.label: Two spots
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive pale or whitish spots that give this species its name, typically visible on the face or thorax depending on the angle

idTips.label: Fuzzy body
idTips.description: Dense, soft hair covers the body with a texture like velvet when viewed up close, often appearing golden-brown or tawny in sunlight

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Males hover and dart around flowers with an energetic, almost frantic flight style, their long antennae trailing behind them

idTips.label: Pollen-covered females
idTips.description: Females often appear dusty with colorful pollen on their leg hairs and belly, creating a fuzzy, powder-puff appearance

habitat: Look for Two-spotted Longhorn Bees in sunny, open areas with diverse wildflowers - old fields, meadows, prairie remnants, and pollinator gardens are prime spots. They're particularly fond of areas with native plants like asters, goldenrod, and sunflowers. You'll often find them in disturbed soils where females can excavate their ground nests, such as along trail edges, garden borders, or south-facing banks.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active in early spring, as this species emerges later in the year than many other native bees.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from mid to late summer when adults emerge and begin foraging. Males can be seen hovering around flowers and potential nest sites, while females actively collect pollen and nectar.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall, especially on warm, sunny days. Late-season flowers like asters and goldenrod are particularly attractive to these bees as they prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard frosts, but their eggs or larvae overwinter safely in underground nest chambers, developing slowly until the following summer.

funFact: Male longhorn bees often sleep communally by grabbing onto plant stems with their jaws and dangling in clusters overnight - you might find a whole group of them hanging like tiny furry ornaments from a single flower stem on cool mornings!
confusionNotes: The biggest challenge is distinguishing this species from other longhorn bees in the same genus, which all share the males' dramatically long antennae. Focus on the "two spots" - those pale markings are your best bet for a positive ID, though you may need a close look or good photo to see them clearly.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "longhorn" bees, these insects are not related to longhorn beetles at all - the name simply refers to their antenna length. They're also sometimes called "long-horned" bees with a hyphen, and both spellings are correct.
compareHints: Among the nine other Melissodes species in New England, the Two-spotted Longhorn Bee is distinguished primarily by those diagnostic pale spots. While all male longhorn bees have impressively long antennae, the specific markings and often the flower preferences help separate the species. The Common Longhorn Bee is probably the most similar, but lacks the distinctive two-spot pattern that gives bimaculatus its name.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Melissodes relatives, Drury's Long-horned Bee is distinguished by its rustic brown coloration and preference for a wide variety of late-season flowers.

Among its Melissodes relatives, the Dark-veined Longhorn Bee stands out for having the most conspicuous dark wing veins - while Common Longhorn Bees and Two-spotted Longhorn Bees have similar body shapes and fuzzy appearance, their wing veins are typically lighter and less noticeable.

Eastern Thistle Longhorn Bees are best distinguished from their Melissodes cousins by their timing and flower preferences - they're active later in summer than most relatives and show a strong preference for thistle flowers.
Among its longhorn bee relatives, the Denticulate Longhorn Bee is most reliably distinguished by its strong association with ironweed flowers rather than physical features alone.
